On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me,' and so on.

From the end of 1811, Western Europe armed and massed its forces more and more intensely, and in 1812 those forces — millions of men, counting the ones who carried supplies and fed the army — set out from the west and moved east toward the Russian frontier. Since 1811 the Russian forces had been drawn toward that same frontier. On the twelfth of June, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed it and war began. In other words, something happened that ran against human reason and human nature. Millions of men committed against one another countless crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, issues of counterfeit money, burglaries, arsons, and murders — more than the records of all the law courts in the world could hold in whole centuries — and at the time the men who committed them did not regard them as crimes.

Napoleon left Dresden on the twenty-ninth of May, after three weeks there among a court of princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before he went, he rewarded the emperor, kings, and princes who deserved it and scolded those he was unhappy with. To the Empress of Austria he gave pearls and diamonds that were his own — that is, ones he had taken from other kings. And, as his historian tells us, he embraced the Empress Marie Louise tenderly. She regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris, and she was left grieving by the parting, which she seemed hardly able to bear. The diplomats still firmly believed peace was possible and worked zealously for it, and Napoleon himself wrote Alexander a letter, addressing him as Monsieur mon frère and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him. Even so, he set off to join his army, and at every station he issued fresh orders to hurry his troops along from west to east. He rode in a coach and six, with pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort around him, on the road through Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Königsberg. In every one of these towns, thousands of people greeted him with excitement and enthusiasm.

"What could he wish or look for that he would not have got through my friendship?" demanded Napoleon, shrugging his shoulders in perplexity. "But no, he has preferred to surround himself with my enemies — and with whom? With Steins, Armfeldts, Bennigsens, Wintzingerodes! Stein, a traitor driven out of his own country; Armfeldt, a rake and an intriguer; Wintzingerode, a fugitive French subject; Bennigsen, rather more of a soldier than the others, but all the same an incompetent who could do nothing in 1807, and who ought to awaken terrible memories in the Emperor Alexander's mind.... Granted, if they were competent they might be made use of," Napoleon continued. He could hardly keep pace in words with the rush of thoughts that kept springing up, all proving how right and strong he was (in his mind the two were one and the same). "But they aren't even that! They are fit neither for war nor for peace! Barclay is said to be the ablest of them all, but judging by his first movements I cannot say so. And what are they doing, all these courtiers? Pfuel proposes, Armfeldt argues, Bennigsen considers, and Barclay, called on to act, does not know what to decide, and time passes and brings no result. Bagration alone is a military man. He's stupid, but he has experience, a quick eye and resolution.... And what part is your young monarch playing in that monstrous crowd? They compromise him and make him answerable for everything that happens. A sovereign should not be with the army unless he is a general!" Napoleon said, evidently flinging these words as a direct challenge to the Emperor. He knew how much Alexander wanted to be a military commander.

His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy man usually thinks of, feels and remembers countless things at once. Yet he has the power and the will to pick one train of thoughts or events and fix his whole attention on it. A healthy man can tear himself away from his deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who comes in, and then go back to his own thoughts. In that respect Prince Andrew's mind was not normal. All its powers were more active and clearer than ever, but they worked apart from his will. The most varied thoughts and images filled his mind at the same time. At moments his brain suddenly worked with a vigor, clarity and depth it had never reached when he was well. Then, in the middle of that work, it would veer off to some unexpected idea, and he had no strength to turn it back.

Pierre ran through various yards and side streets with his small burden and got back to the Gruzinski garden at the corner of the Povarskoy. At first he did not recognize the place he had set out from to look for the child. He could not, because it was now so crowded with people and with goods dragged out of the houses. Russian families had taken refuge there from the fire with their belongings, and among them were several French soldiers in assorted clothing. Pierre paid them no attention. He hurried to find the civil servant's family, so he could give the daughter back to her mother and go off to save someone else. Pierre felt he still had a great deal to do, and had to do it fast. He was flushed from the heat and the running, and at that moment he felt more strongly than ever the youth, vitality and resolve that had come over him when he ran to save the child. She had gone quiet now. She clung to Pierre's coat with her little hands and sat on his arm looking around her like a small wild animal. He glanced at her now and then with a faint smile. He thought he saw something touchingly innocent in that frightened, sickly little face.

Suddenly there was a crackling, rolling roar that seemed to him louder than the most terrible thunder, and he looked around. There was some smoke, and the Frenchmen, pale and with trembling hands, were busy near the pit. Two more prisoners were brought forward. These two looked around vainly at the onlookers in the same way, with the same look, silently begging for protection. They plainly could not understand or believe what was going to happen to them. They could not believe it because they alone knew what their lives meant to them, and so they neither understood nor believed that anyone could take them away.
